description: We are Comic Drift, a team of students passionate about space exploration, technology, and innovation. For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we developed Root Cause, an interactive game where young players investigate emergencies at a Martian outpost using real NASA data. Through scientific experiments, resource management, and critical decisions, we aim to make space science engaging and accessible while inspiring the next generation of scientists, engineers, and explorers.
summary:
Something is wrong at the Mars base, and it is your job to find out what it is. Root Cause is a browser game for kids aged 7–12. Players are flight controllers at Suhail Base in Gale Crater, Mars. Each case starts with an alarm. Looking at the readings is free, but every test costs crew hours. To win, players must think like scientists: predict, test, rule things out and fix the real cause.

The six cases cover power, food, life support and radiation shielding, and show how the systems depend on each other. A weak battery leads to the heater being cut, the greenhouse freezing, and the lettuce stopping growing. Asking Mission Control costs crew hours too, because messages take 4 to 24 minutes each way between Earth and Mars. The game uses real NASA data from InSight, Curiosity and DONKI, every case ends with the true NASA story it is based on, and it runs in any browser in English, Arabic, French and Spanish.
details:
HOW A CASE WORKS

1. Alarm. Something is wrong. Press the master alarm to start.

2. Quick decision. A trade-off with no free option. For example: switch the lab off to save battery (and lose a sol of science), or keep it running (and risk the greenhouse heater being cut tonight).

3. Look at the readings. Free charts of the outpost's systems, with a dotted "normal day" line to compare against.

4. Run tests. Each test costs crew hours. Before it runs, the player predicts the result.

5. Ask Mission Control if stuck. It costs 2 crew hours, because messages take 4 to 24 minutes each way between Earth and Mars.

6. Call the root cause. A wrong call costs 2 hours.

7. Build the chain. Put the cause-and-effect steps in order. One card is fake, and a wrong card costs an hour.

8. Fix it. Some fixes only treat the symptom. Only fixing the cause closes the case.

9. Real mission. Each case ends with the true NASA story it is based on, with a link.

Stars are awarded for fixing the problem, using few tests, and predicting every test correctly. The root cause is picked at random from 2–3 possibilities each time, so replaying a case can lead to a different answer.

THE SIX CASES

1. Dim Day (tutorial), power: dust slowly covered InSight's solar panels (2018–2022).

2. Cold Lettuce, food and power: a dust storm put InSight into safe mode (January 2022).

3. Stuffy Air, life support (CO₂): Apollo 13's CO₂ filter fix (1970).

4. Oxygen Alarm, life support (oxygen): the ISS ammonia false alarm (January 2015).

5. Slow Leak, life support (air pressure): the ISS slow air leak hunt (2020).

6. Storm Incoming, radiation shielding: the solar storm that hit Mars (May 20, 2024).

HOW IT FITS THE CHALLENGE

- Life support, radiation shielding, power and food: each has at least one case, and cases show how the systems depend on each other. A weak battery leads to the heater being cut, the greenhouse freezing, and the lettuce stopping growing.

- Communication delay: Ask Mission Control costs crew hours because of the real Earth–Mars message delay.

- No free choices: tests, wrong calls, wrong chain cards, wrong fixes and asking for help all cost crew hours. Every quick decision has a downside on purpose, because real mission planners never get a free choice.

- Replayability: random root causes, plus stars to improve on.

- Plain language: short sentences. Words like sol, ppm, kPa and ohms are explained next to the chart where they appear.

- Low barrier: runs in any browser, with no download or sign-up needed.

- Four languages: English, Arabic, French and Spanish.

NASA DATA USED

All of this is also listed in the game under "NASA data used" on the title screen.

- InSight lander solar power: about 5,000 Wh per sol after landing (2018), cut by dust to about 500 by spring 2022. Used in Dim Day's "InSight's solar power" reading.

- Curiosity rover REMS weather station: Gale Crater, sol 4189 (May 19, 2024): low −68 °C, high −5 °C, 861 Pa. Sol 4190 (May 20, 2024): low −69 °C, high −3 °C, 860 Pa. Used in the "Air outside" reading in every case.

- DONKI space weather database: CME 2024-05-20T05:36:00-CME-001, from Sun region 13664, about 2,678 km/s. Used in Storm Incoming's space weather alert from Mission Control.

- Curiosity rover RAD radiation detector: 8,100 micrograys on May 20, 2024 (about 30 chest X-rays), against about 180–225 on a normal sol. Used in Storm Incoming's "Radiation dose" reading.

- Earth–Mars message delay: 4 to 24 minutes each way. Used for Ask Mission Control.

- Real mission stories: Apollo 13, InSight and the ISS, in the "Real mission" box at the end of each case.

This is archived data stored in the game, not a live feed. The outpost's own readings (battery, greenhouse, CO₂ and so on) come from a simple simulation (js/sim.js), so each case behaves in a consistent, realistic way.

PLAYTESTING

21 people played the game and filled in a feedback form. 62% were in our target age of 7–12, and 67% rated the game 4 or 5 out of 5 for being easy to play. 5 of the 7 who played in another language rated the translation 4 or 5 out of 5, and nobody rated it below 3. Two of the three written suggestions asked for clearer instructions, and one asked for more levels. We listened and made significant changes to help with the gameplay: we addressed these complaints by adding a tutorial and instructions.

HOW IT'S BUILT

Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no frameworks, libraries or build step. Sounds are generated in code with the Web Audio API.

- index.html: screens and layout

- css/style.css: mission-control look and visuals

- js/cases.js: the six cases (readings, tests, causes, fixes, costs)

- js/sim.js: 48-hour outpost simulation and chart data

- js/game.js: game logic

- js/graph.js: chart drawing

- js/sound.js: sound effects

- js/lang/*.js: all game text in English, Arabic, French and Spanish


## Use of SI

We used Claude (Anthropic) explicitily for:

- **Translations:** the Arabic, French and Spanish versions of all game text. The game says this on the title screen.

- **One bug fix:** a logic error in the chart drawing (`js/graph.js`) which we could not fix by ourselves..

- **Review and testing:** Claude reviewed the game against the challenge brief, found bugs, tested every case in every language, Our team built these changes ourselves.
